parts.problem_md: Define the term standard electrode potential.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Standard electrode potential is the:
> 
> - Electrode potential of a half-cell measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) **[1 mark]**
> - Measured under standard conditions (298 K, 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, 101 kPa / 1 atm) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The definition has two components:
> 
> 1. What it is measured against
> 
>   - The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), which is assigned a value of 0 V
> 2. The conditions under which it is measured:
> 
>   - 298 K, 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ion concentration, and 101 kPa.
> 
> Both parts are needed for full marks.

parts.problem_md:
A current of 1.50 A is passed through aqueous CuSO<sub>4</sub> for 25.0 minutes.

Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode:

- List the known values:

  - current, *I* = 1.50 A
  - time, *t* = 25.0 min = 1500 s
  - Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *M*<sub>r</sub> of copper = 63.5
- Calculate the charge passed, *Q*:

*Q* = *I* x *t*

*Q* = 1.50 x 1500

*Q* = 2250 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of electrons transferred:

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = $\frac{Q}{F}$

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = $\frac{2250}{9.65\times10^{4}}$

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = 0.02332 mol **[1 mark]**

- Use the half-equation to find the mass of copper deposited:

Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu (s)

n(Cu) = 0.02332 ÷ 2 = 0.01166 mol

mass = 0.01166 x 63.5

mass = **0.740 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always convert time to seconds before calculating charge: 25.0 minutes x 60 = 1500 s. The ratio of electrons to copper atoms comes from the half-equation Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu (s), which shows 2 mol of electrons are needed to deposit 1 mol of copper.

parts.problem_md: Use the Nernst equation from the Data Booklet to calculate the electrode potential (*E*) for the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell where [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.50 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> and [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.77 V). Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the electrode potential of the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell:

- List the known values:

  - *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>) = +0.77 V
  - [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.50 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - *z* = 1 (one electron transferred: Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>)
- Substitute into the Nernst equation:

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + `open parentheses fraction numerator 0.059 over denominator z end fraction close parentheses` log<sub>10</sub> `fraction numerator left square bracket oxidised space species right square bracket over denominator left square bracket reduced space species right square bracket end fraction`

*E* = 0.77 + $\frac{0.059}{1}$ log<sub>10</sub> $\frac{0.50}{0.01}$ **[1 mark]**

*E* = 0.77 + 0.059 x log<sub>10</sub> (50)

*E* = 0.77 + (0.059 x 1.699)

*E* = 0.77 + 0.100

*E* = **+0.870 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Check that the oxidised species ([Fe<sup>3+</sup>]) is in the numerator and the reduced species ([Fe<sup>2+</sup>]) is in the denominator of the log term. Here *z* = 1 since only one electron is transferred in the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-equation. The simplified Nernst constant of 0.059 only applies at 298 K.

parts.problem_md:
A cell is constructed using the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu half-cells under standard conditions. The equation for the overall cell reaction is shown.

2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

The standard cell potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>, for this reaction is +0.43 V.

Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Give your answer in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to three significant figures. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction:

- List the known values:

  - *n* = 2 (2 mol of electrons transferred per mol of Cu oxidised)
  - *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = +0.43 V
- Apply the equation:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −*nFE*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −2 x (9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup>) x 0.43

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −82 990 J mol<sup>-1</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Convert to kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −$\frac{82990}{1000}$

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **−83.0 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Don't drop the minus sign. A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> gives a negative Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, confirming the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.
> 
> Remember *n* is the number of moles of electrons transferred per mole of reaction as written. Here 2 mol of Fe<sup>3+</sup> are each reduced by 1 electron, so *n* = 2.

This question is about electrochemical cells.

**Fig. 1.1** shows the apparatus used to measure the standard electrode potential, *E*^θ^, of a cell composed of a Cu(II)/Cu half-cell and an Fe(II)/Fe half-cell.

In the spaces below, identify what the four letters **A**–**D** in **Fig. 1.1** represent.

parts.solution_md:
The four letters in Fig. 1.1 represent:

| **A** | copper / Cu electrode |
|---|---|
| **B** | iron / Fe electrode |
| **C** | 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution containing Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions (e.g. CuSO<sub>4</sub>) |
| **D** | 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution containing Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions (e.g. FeSO<sub>4</sub>) |

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for A = copper / Cu electrode
> 
> 1 mark for B = iron / Fe electrode
> 
> 1 mark for C = 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution containing Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions (e.g. CuSO<sub>4</sub>)
> 
> 1 mark for D = 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution containing Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions (e.g. FeSO<sub>4</sub>)
> 
> (A and B) and (C and D) are interchangeable
> 
> The solution for C must correspond to the metal stated for A and the solution for D must correspond to the metal stated for B

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both half-cells are metal / metal ion half-cells, so the electrode is the metal itself and the solution contains an aqueous solution of the corresponding metal ion.
> 
> Since this is a standard electrode potential measurement, all solution concentrations must be 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>. Any appropriate Cu<sup>2+</sup> or Fe<sup>2+</sup> salt is accepted.

parts.problem_md:
The standard electrode potentials of the two half-cells are as follows.

Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe  *E*<sup>θ</sup> = −0.44 V

Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu  *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.34 V

i) Identify which electrode acts as the negative electrode.

[1]

ii) Construct the overall equation for this electrochemical cell.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The electrode that acts as the negative electrode is:
> 
> - Iron / Fe **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The overall equation for this electrochemical cell is:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Fe(s) ⇌ Cu(s) + Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The half-cell with the more negative standard electrode potential acts as the negative electrode and undergoes oxidation. Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = −0.44 V) is more negative than Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.34 V), so iron is the negative electrode.
> 
> Electrons flow from the negative electrode (Fe) to the positive electrode (Cu) through the external circuit.
> 
> To construct the overall equation, reverse the iron half-equation for oxidation and add to the copper reduction half-equation:
> 
> - Reduction: Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu(s)
> - Oxidation: Fe(s) ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> - Overall: Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Fe(s) ⇌ Cu(s) + Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq)

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The standard electrode potentials of the two half-cells are as follows.

Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe  E° = −0.44 V

Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu  E° = +0.34 V

The overall equation for this electrochemical cell is:

Cu²⁺(aq) + Fe(s) ⇌ Cu(s) + Fe²⁺(aq)

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> of this cell is +0.78 V.

State whether this reaction is feasible. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether this reaction is feasible:
> 
> - Feasible **[1 mark]**
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> is positive **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction is feasible (thermodynamically likely to occur) when the standard cell potential *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> is positive. A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> means the forward reaction releases energy and can proceed under standard conditions.

parts.problem_md:
The standard electrode potentials for seven different redox systems are shown in **Table 3.1**.

**Table 3.1**

| **redox system** | **equation** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | 2H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> (g) | 0.00 |
| **2** | Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) | +0.77 |
| **3** | Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu(s) | +0.34 |
| **4** | Cl<sub>2</sub>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2Cl<sup>–</sup>(aq) | +1.36 |
| **5** | O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 4e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2H<sub>2</sub>O(l) | +1.23 |
| **6** | Al<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + 3e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Al(s) | −1.66 |
| **7** | I<sub>2</sub>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2I<sup>–</sup>(aq) | +0.54 |

An electrochemical cell can be made based on redox systems **2** and **3**.

i) Construct the overall equation for the cell reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate the voltage of this cell.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The overall equation for the cell reaction is:
> 
> - 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The voltage of this cell is:
> 
> - *E*<sub>cell</sub> (= 0.77 − 0.34) = 0.43 V **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Redox system 2 (Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>, +0.77 V) is more positive than system 3 (Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu, +0.34 V), so Fe<sup>3+</sup> is more readily reduced and acts as the oxidising agent. Cu undergoes oxidation.
> 
> To construct the overall equation, write Fe<sup>3+</sup> as reduced (forward) and Cu as oxidised (reverse), multiply to balance electrons, then cancel:
> 
> - 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)
> - Cu (s) → Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> - Overall: 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

| **3** | Cu^2+^(aq) + 2e^–^ ⇌ Cu(s) | +0.34 |

| **7** | I~2~(aq) + 2e^–^ ⇌ 2I^–^(aq) | +0.54 |

i) Using redox systems **5**, **6** and **7** **only** in **Table 3.1**, construct the overall equations for **three** reactions that might be feasible.

[3]

ii) Give **two** reasons why these reactions might not take place, even if they are feasible.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) The overall equations for **three** reactions that might be feasible are:

- 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 12H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 4Al (s) → 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 4Al<sup>3+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
- 3I<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2Al (s) → 2Al<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 6I<sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
- O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 4I<sup>–</sup> (aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 2I<sub>2</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**

ii) **Two** reasons why these reactions might not take place, even if they are feasible:

- The rate of reaction is slow / *E*<sub>a</sub> is high **[1 mark]**
- Suitable conditions (e.g. catalyst, temperature) are not available **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> For part (i), any three of the three equations above are required. State symbols must be correct throughout for the mark to be awarded.
> 
> For part (ii), allow any two kinetic / conditions-based reasons. Do not accept 'the conditions are not standard' or 'concentration is not 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>' as a reason for a feasible reaction not proceeding because thermodynamic feasibility already accounts for standard conditions.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction being thermodynamically feasible (positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>) means it is energetically downhill, but this says nothing about the rate. Many feasible reactions have high activation energies and proceed extremely slowly without a catalyst.
> 
> For the three equations, the possible combinations from systems 5, 6, and 7 are: 5 & 6, 6 & 7, and 5 & 7.

Calculate the electrode potential at 298 K of redox system **3** if the concentration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) ions was 0.0002 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the electrode potential of redox system 3 at non-standard conditions:

- State the Nernst equation (from the Data Booklet) and identify the variables:

*E*<sup>θ</sup>(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu) = +0.34 V

z = 2

[Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.0002 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

The reduced species is the solid metal Cu, which has no concentration term, so the equation simplifies to:

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + `\frac{0.059}{z}\log_{10}[\text{Cu}^{2+}]`

- Substitute values:

*E* = 0.34 + $\frac{0.059}{2} \mathrm{log}_{10} ( 0 . 0002 )$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the logarithm term:

log<sub>10</sub>(0.0002) = −3.699

- Solve the equation:

*E* = 0.34 + (0.0295 x −3.699)

*E* = 0.34 − 0.109 **[1 mark]**

**Extract:**

The standard electrode potential for Zn^2+^ (aq) + 2e^–^ → Zn (s) is –0.76 V.

Calculate the length of time, in hours, required to deposit 1.0 g of zinc on the item to be electroplated. Assume the current is a constant 0.1 A throughout this period.

State your answer to 3 significant figures and show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the time required to deposit 1.0 g of zinc:

- List the known values:

  - mass of Zn = 1.0 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub> of Zn = 65.4 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - current, *I* = 0.1 A
  - Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculate the moles of Zn required:

n(Zn) = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

n(Zn) = $\frac{1.0}{65.4}$

n(Zn) = 0.01529 mol

- Calculate the moles of electrons required:

Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Zn (s)

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = 0.01529 × 2

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = 0.03058 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge required, *Q*:

*Q* = n(e<sup>-</sup>) × *F*

*Q* = 0.03058 × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup>

*Q* = 2951 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the time and convert to hours:

*t* = $\frac{Q}{I}$

*t *= $\frac{2951}{0.1}$

*t *= 29 510 s

- Convert to hours:

*t* = $\frac{29510}{3600}$

*t* = **8.20 hours** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to convert time from seconds to hours at the end by dividing by 3600 (60 × 60).
> 
> The number of moles of electrons comes from the half-equation Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Zn (s), which shows 2 mol of electrons are needed per mol of zinc deposited.

parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md:
The standard electrode potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup>, of the Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) / Ag (s) half-cell is +0.80 V.

Use the Nernst equation from the Data Booklet to calculate the concentration of silver ions, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, in this half-cell. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the concentration of silver ions in the half-cell:

- List the known values:

  - *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Ag<sup>+</sup>/Ag) = +0.80 V
  - *E* = +0.72 V
  - *z* = 1 (one electron transferred: Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Ag)
  - temperature = 25 °C = 298 K
- Substitute into the Nernst equation:

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + (0.059/*z*) log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)]

0.72 = 0.80 + (0.059/1) log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange to find log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup>]:

log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = (0.72 − 0.80) ÷ 0.059

log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = −0.08 ÷ 0.059 = −1.356 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [Ag<sup>+</sup>]:

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = 10<sup>−1.356</sup>

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = **0.0440 mol dm**<sup>**−3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 1-electron half-reaction (Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Ag), *z* = 1, so the Nernst equation simplifies to *E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + 0.059 log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup>].
> 
> Since [Ag<sup>+</sup>] < 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, the log term is negative, making *E* less than *E*<sup>θ</sup> which is consistent with the measured value of +0.72 V being lower than the standard value of +0.80 V.

The student set up the cell between redox systems **2** and **3** again. This time, they did not dilute the solution of redox system **3** but they used a solution of 0.01 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> of Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions for redox system **2**. The temperature remained at 298 K.

Calculate the electrode potential, *E*, for redox system **2** under these conditions. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the electrode potential for redox system 2 at non-standard conditions:

- Identify the variables:

  - *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Cr<sup>3+</sup>/Cr) = −0.74 V
  - z = 3
  - [Cr<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>
- Substitute into the Nernst equation (Data Booklet):

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + `\frac{0.059}{z} \log_{10}[\text{Cr}^{3+}]`

*E* = −0.74 + $\frac{0.059}{3} \mathrm{log}_{10} ( 0 . 01 )$ **[1 mark]**

- Solve for *E*:

log<sub>10</sub>(0.01) = −2

*E* = −0.74 + (0.01967 × −2) = −0.74 − 0.0393

*E* = **−0.78 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow −0.7793 V (4 sf)
> 
> Allow error carried forward if correct method but arithmetic error

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Nernst equation is in the Data Booklet. Since Cr is a solid, the reduced species has no concentration term, so [oxidised species]/[reduced species] simplifies to [Cr<sup>3+</sup>].
> 
> Since [Cr<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> < 1.0 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>, log<sub>10</sub>[Cr<sup>3+</sup>] is negative, so *E* is more negative than *E*<sup>θ</sup>.
